notes.title: Chapter map: Async I/O
notes.html:
One thread, one event loop, many suspended coroutines: every note is either the loop, what it drives, or how to live with code that doesn't cooperate. Read each arrow as a sentence: tasks built on async / await.

Green = CORE, blue = SUPPORTING, yellow = BREADTH, grey = another chapter (dashed edges).

Reading order: 40 event loop ─▶ 41 async / await ─▶ 42 tasks & cancellation ─▶ 43 bridging ─▶ 44 primitives ─▶ 45 ecosystem

  • The one big idea: tasks switch only at an await that really waits. That one rule explains the wins (thousands of cheap concurrent waits, no races between awaits) and the hazards (one blocking call freezes every task, races appear across await points, cancellation arrives only at an await).
  • The two most-confused pairs: gather vs TaskGroup (42: on failure, siblings keep running vs get cancelled) · non-blocking vs to_thread (43: the operation yields vs a different thread blocks).
  • Ten minutes before an interview: 40's shared-fate picture and sequence diagram, 42's gather vs TaskGroup picture, then 41's coroutine lifecycle.
  • Cross-chapter: generators (the suspended frame coroutines are made of) · concurrency vs parallelism (async is pure concurrency) · the concurrency chapter map (its decision tree says when asyncio is the right model).

No decision tree here: these notes build on each other. Whether to use asyncio at all is the first tree in the concurrency chapter map.

notes.title: The Async Execution Model
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 A conceptual overview of asyncio · 📘 asyncio event loop · 📘 Developing with asyncio · 📜 PEP 3156 · 📖 GeeksforGeeks: asyncio in Python

⚡ TL;DR

Threads wait in place; an event loop parks each wait as a small object and runs whoever is ready. Tasks switch only at an await that really waits, so one blocking call freezes every task on the loop.

🧭 Flow: create_task(coro) ─▶ loop steps the task until an await on an unfinished future ─▶ the task suspends ─▶ loop asks the selector which sockets are ready, until the next timer ─▶ a future completes ─▶ its task is scheduled ─▶ it resumes at the await

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
Is asyncio parallel? No: one thread, concurrency only; tasks interleave at await points.
What does one loop iteration do? Wait on the selector until the next timer, then run every ready callback.
When does a task switch? Only at an await on something unfinished, never between other statements.
Why does one blocking call slow every endpoint? It holds the only thread; no other task can resume.
How do you detect blocking? Loop-lag metric in production; debug=True in staging logs callbacks over 100 ms.
✏️ Draw by hand: one await round trip loop steps task → task awaits future, suspends → selector reports socket → future done → task resumes.

💡 The idea

Five 100 ms network calls in a row take half a second, almost all of it blocked in the kernel. Write them as coroutines and run them as tasks:

import asyncio, time
async def fetch():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)          # a non-blocking wait: control goes back to the loop
    return 1
async def main():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    tasks = [asyncio.create_task(fetch()) for _ in range(5)]
    [await t for t in tasks]
    print(f"{time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s")   # → 0.10s
asyncio.run(main())

Five waits overlapped on one thread, and it scales: 10,000 concurrent asyncio.sleep(0.2) calls finished in about 0.25 s (CPython 3.12). Now put one time.sleep(0.3) inside a coroutine and watch an unrelated task:

The trade: async swaps a thread per wait for a small object per wait, and in exchange every coroutine on the loop must yield at await, because one blocking call freezes all of them.

⚙️ How it works

One await that has to wait, end to end:

The loop never pre-empts anyone; it only resumes tasks whose futures are done. The rules that follow:

Rule What actually happens
One loop, one thread, one ready queue Each iteration computes how long it may block (zero if callbacks are ready, else until the earliest timer), asks the selector (kqueue on macOS, epoll on Linux) which sockets are ready, then runs every ready callback to completion.
Tasks are callbacks that resume coroutines A Task steps its coroutine to the next await on an unfinished Future; the frame suspends like a generator's. asyncio.sleep(0.1) is a timer that completes a future 100 ms later.
Switches happen only at await Code between two awaits runs uninterrupted: no thread can interleave there (fewer races), and CPU work or a blocking call there holds the loop. asyncio.sleep(0) is an explicit "let others run".
Blocking is detectable asyncio.run(main(), debug=True) logs callbacks slower than loop.slow_callback_duration (100 ms): on 3.12 a time.sleep(0.15) logged "Executing <Task …> took 0.152 seconds".
Still one thread under the GIL Concurrency, never parallelism (concurrency vs parallelism); CPU work belongs in a process pool or GIL-releasing native code.

💻 Code

The most useful production instrument for an async service: an event-loop lag monitor, plus debug mode in staging.

import asyncio, logging, os, time
log = logging.getLogger("loop")

async def monitor_loop_lag(interval: float = 0.25, warn_ms: float = 50.0) -> None:
    while True:                                  # how late does a 250 ms sleep wake?
        start = time.perf_counter()
        await asyncio.sleep(interval)
        lag_ms = (time.perf_counter() - start - interval) * 1000
        LOOP_LAG_MS.observe(lag_ms)              # export as a histogram
        if lag_ms > warn_ms:
            log.warning("event loop lag %.1f ms: a callback blocked the loop", lag_ms)

async def main() -> None:
    lag_task = asyncio.create_task(monitor_loop_lag(), name="loop-lag")   # keep a reference
    await serve_forever()

asyncio.run(main(), debug=bool(int(os.environ.get("ASYNC_DEBUG", "0"))))   # staging: debug

A blocking call anywhere shows up as a lag spike everywhere. Keep the task in a variable: the loop holds only weak references to tasks, so an unreferenced one can be garbage-collected mid-run.

⚠️ Break it: a heartbeat that should wake every 10 ms, next to a handler that blocks.

import asyncio, time
async def heartbeat(lags):
    for _ in range(40):
        t = time.perf_counter(); await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
        lags.append((time.perf_counter() - t - 0.01) * 1000)
async def handler(blocking):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
    time.sleep(0.3) if blocking else await asyncio.sleep(0.3)
async def main(blocking):
    lags = []; await asyncio.gather(heartbeat(lags), handler(blocking)); return max(lags)
print(f"{asyncio.run(main(False)):.1f} ms, {asyncio.run(main(True)):.1f} ms")
# look for: the second number near 300 ms, though heartbeat never called time.sleep
# naive model predicts: both near 0, the blocking call is in a different coroutine

On CPython 3.12 it printed 1.2 ms, 299.1 ms. The loop is shared fate: in a web service the heartbeat is every other in-flight request.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: asyncio runs many coroutines on one thread. When a coroutine awaits something that isn't ready, it suspends and the event loop runs whichever task is ready, resuming the first when its future completes. That overlaps thousands of network waits cheaply. The catch: switches happen only at await, so a blocking call or CPU work between awaits freezes every task on the loop.

Q · Mechanism — Walk through one loop iteration. Where does asyncio.sleep fit? The loop works out how long it may block, calls the selector with that timeout, schedules callbacks for ready sockets and expired timers, then runs every ready callback (the sequence diagram). asyncio.sleep(d) creates a future and a timer that completes it after d seconds, then awaits it, so the task suspends and the loop stays free. time.sleep(d) blocks the thread in the kernel instead, which is the 300 ms of lag in Break it.

Q · Failure — p99 spikes to 300 ms on all endpoints of an async API, but only one endpoint changed. Diagnose. The changed endpoint doesn't yield: a sync HTTP client, a sync DB driver, a file read, or CPU work like a big JSON parse. It holds the worker's only thread, so every request on that worker waits. Prove it with per-worker loop lag lining up with the spikes, debug mode in staging naming the coroutine, or py-spy dump showing the blocking stack (3.14 adds python -m asyncio ps). Fix: an async client, [[07-async-io/43-bridging-sync-async|asyncio.to_thread]] for unavoidable blocking I/O, a process pool for CPU.

Q · Design — Serve 10,000 concurrent LLM streaming connections. Why asyncio, and where does it break? It's almost pure waiting, so coroutines beat threads: an ASGI server, httpx.AsyncClient with a bounded pool, SSE to clients via async generators, a few worker processes per host with a connection cap each. It breaks wherever something holds the loop: per-token work must stay tiny, and moderation, embeddings or large prompt assembly go to a process pool. Each stream needs a bounded buffer for slow clients and a cancellation path on disconnect (cancellation). I'd watch per-worker loop lag first: it moves before p99.

⚖️ Compare

Threads asyncio Processes
Switching pre-emptive (OS + GIL) cooperative, at await only independent
Cost per concurrent wait a thread and its stack a task object a whole process
A blocking call… blocks one thread blocks every task on the loop blocks one worker
Races between any two bytecodes only across await points none on Python objects
CPU parallelism no (GIL) no yes
Libraries any must be async-aware any

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "Async code runs in parallel"
    ✅ One thread, one task at a time: it overlaps waiting, never two pieces of Python.
    ↳ So: CPU-bound work needs processes, not coroutines.
  • 🪞 "A slow call in one coroutine only slows that request"
    ✅ A blocking call holds the loop's only thread, so every task waits (see Break it).
  • ❌ "async def makes a function non-blocking"
    ✅ It only makes it a coroutine.
    ↳ Why: if the body calls blocking code, it blocks the loop; only awaiting genuinely async operations yields.
  • 🔀 Not the same as threads
    ↳ Difference: both are concurrency; the OS decides when threads switch, your awaits decide for async.
    ↳ So: async needs async-aware libraries; threads don't.
  • ⚠️ Don't create tasks without keeping a reference.
    ↳ Why: the loop holds only weak references, so an unreferenced task can vanish mid-run.
    ↳ Instead: store it, or use a TaskGroup (tasks).
  • ⚠️ Don't put CPU work in asyncio.to_thread and call it solved.
    ↳ Why: the thread still competes for the GIL with the loop.
    ↳ Instead: a process pool, or native code that releases the GIL.

How the asyncio API has moved (measurements in this note: CPython 3.12.13 and 3.14.6, macOS arm64):

🕸️ Connections

Path: concurrency vs parallelism ─▶ async execution model ─▶ async / await ─▶ tasks & cancellation ─▶ bridging sync and async

  • Builds on generators: a suspended task is a parked frame, resumed by the loop instead of next().
  • Contrasts with threading: a thread per wait and pre-emptive switching, versus a task per wait and switches only at await.
  • Used by tasks and cancellation and async primitives: everything else in the chapter runs on this loop.
  • Breaks when combined with blocking libraries: requests, sync DB drivers and CPU work all hold the loop (bridging has the fixes).
  • Same idea elsewhere: Node.js runs JavaScript on one event loop with the same "never block the loop" rule.

notes.title: async/await & Coroutine Objects
notes.html:
📚 References

📜 PEP 492: async and await · 📘 Coroutines and Tasks: awaitables · 📜 PEP 342: coroutines via enhanced generators · 📖 Super Fast Python: asyncio guide

⚡ TL;DR

Calling an async def builds a paused coroutine; only await (or a Task) runs it. await passes the wait up to the loop and hands back the result: forget it and the work silently never happens.

🧭 Flow: fetch() returns a coroutine object, body not run ─▶ await or a Task calls send(None) ─▶ body runs to an await on an unfinished future ─▶ suspends, the future goes up to the loop ─▶ future done, send() resumes it ─▶ return x arrives as StopIteration(x), the value of the await

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
What does calling an async def return? A coroutine object, frame parked before line 1; the body hasn't run.
How is a coroutine driven? send(None) to the next suspension; completion raises StopIteration(value). A Task does it for you.
What's an awaitable? Anything with __await__: coroutines, Tasks, Futures, custom objects.
How is "never awaited" detected? A RuntimeWarning when the unstarted coroutine is garbage-collected, not at the call.
Coroutine vs generator? Same suspended-frame machinery; separate types; not iterable vs not awaitable.
✏️ Draw by hand: the coroutine lifecycle CREATED ─send─▶ RUNNING ─await─▶ SUSPENDED ─send─▶ RUNNING ─return─▶ CLOSED; never awaited → warning at GC.

💡 The idea

Calling a function runs it: by the next line the work is done. Add async and call it the same way:

import asyncio
async def fetch_user(user_id):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)              # a real async client call in practice
    return {"id": user_id}
result = fetch_user(1)                    # → <coroutine object fetch_user at 0x…>
result["id"]                              # → TypeError: 'coroutine' object is not subscriptable

The body didn't run. You got a coroutine object: a paused call, parked before its first line, exactly like calling a generator function. It runs only when something awaits it on an event loop: user = await fetch_user(1) inside another coroutine. Now leave the await out:

async def handler():
    fetch_user(1)                         # forgot await
    return "ok"
asyncio.run(handler())                    # → 'ok', then RuntimeWarning: coroutine 'fetch_user' was never awaited

The handler "succeeded" and the call never happened. The only evidence is a warning printed when the unused coroutine is garbage-collected, after the handler returned (CPython 3.12).

The trade: async def lets a call pause at every await so a loop can interleave it with others, and the price is that calling it only creates the work: you have to await it to get it done.

⚙️ How it works

A coroutine's life, as inspect.getcoroutinestate reports it (verified on CPython 3.12; markers match Break it):

A coroutine is a generator's machinery under a separate type. Which objects you can await and which you can iterate:

Rule What actually happens
A coroutine is a generator in disguise Same suspended frame (cr_frame), send, throw, close. await x is essentially [[03-iterators-generators-comprehensions/16-yield-from-delegation|yield from]] x.__await__(): it delegates down the chain and passes the suspension up to the loop.
But deliberately not a generator Its own type: iter(co) raises 'coroutine' object is not iterable, and awaiting a plain generator raises object generator can't be used in 'await' expression (3.12).
Awaitables Anything with __await__: native coroutines, asyncio.Task and Future, custom objects. Async generators are consumed with async for, not await.
"Never awaited" is a GC-time check Finalising an unstarted coroutine emits the RuntimeWarning; nothing checks at the call site, which is why the bug passes tests.

💻 Code

Guard rails that make forgotten awaits fail loudly, plus one code path for hooks that may be sync or async:

# pyproject.toml
# [tool.pytest.ini_options]
# filterwarnings = ["error::RuntimeWarning"]   # "never awaited" now fails the test
# ruff: RUF006 (unkept create_task), ASYNC rules · mypy: unused coroutine values

import asyncio, inspect

def run_hook(hook, *args):
    result = hook(*args)
    if inspect.isawaitable(result):            # coroutine, Task, Future or custom __await__
        return result
    return asyncio.sleep(0, result=result)     # wrap a plain value so callers always await

async def on_event(hooks, event):
    for hook in hooks:
        await run_hook(hook, event)

Warnings-as-errors turns every forgotten await a test exercises into a failure; checking isawaitable on the result covers every kind of awaitable, not just async def.

⚠️ Break it: drive a coroutine by hand, with no event loop.

import asyncio
async def two():
    print("  body started"); await asyncio.sleep(0); print("  resumed"); return 42
co = two()                                         # ①
print("created:", co)
print("first send ->", co.send(None))              # ②
try: co.send(None)                                 # ③
except StopIteration as e: print("value =", e.value)
# look for: "body started" only at the first send; 42 arrives inside StopIteration
# naive model predicts: "body started" when two() is called, and 42 returned directly

On CPython 3.12 it prints the coroutine object, then body started, first send -> None, resumed, value = 42. The event loop is just code that calls send() when a future completes, so a "stuck" coroutine is one whose future never completed.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: Calling an async def returns a coroutine object and runs nothing; awaiting it, or wrapping it in a Task, runs it. A coroutine is a suspendable frame like a generator: at an await on something unfinished it suspends and the event loop runs other work, then resumes it with the result. The trap is a missing await: the call silently does nothing, and the only sign is a RuntimeWarning at garbage collection.

Q · Mechanism — The event loop is just Python. How does it drive a coroutine forward? It wraps the coroutine in a Task whose step calls coro.send(None). The coroutine runs until an await reaches an unfinished Future at the bottom of the await chain; the future is yielded up the chain and out of send(), and the task registers a done-callback on it. When the future completes, the callback schedules the next step, every suspended frame in the chain resumes, and the innermost await evaluates to the result. return ends it as StopIteration, and the task stores the value.

Q · Failure — Review finds client.post(url) in an async handler with no await. What happens, and why is it easy to miss? The request is never sent: the handler gets a coroutine object, ignores it and returns success, so the system goes inconsistent. Nothing fails; the warning comes at garbage collection, after the return, on stderr that's often filtered. Tests that only check the return value pass. Defences: filterwarnings = error::RuntimeWarning in tests, a type checker, ruff's async rules, and routing warnings into logging in production.

Q · Design — Ship a client library for both sync and async callers without duplicating logic. A sans-I/O core holds request building, signing, retries, parsing and pagination as plain functions; two thin clients (Client over httpx.Client, AsyncClient over httpx.AsyncClient) loop over it with their own transport. Avoid asyncio.run() as a sync wrapper: it fails inside a running loop. Avoid wrapping sync code with to_thread for async callers: a thread per call and no real cancellation (bridging). I'd test first for a sync client called inside a running loop, the path that silently blocks callers.

⚖️ Compare

Generator Native coroutine Async generator
Defined with def + yield async def async def + yield
Calling it returns generator object coroutine object async generator object
Consumed with for, next() await, or a Task async for, anext()
Suspends to its caller, with a value the event loop, via a future the loop, and yields values
Result delivered by StopIteration.value StopIteration.value → await result StopAsyncIteration ends it

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "Calling an async def starts it in the background"
    ✅ It creates a coroutine object and runs nothing.
    ↳ Fix: await it to run it now, asyncio.create_task to run it alongside.
  • 🪞 "A missing await would raise an error"
    ✅ It returns a coroutine and carries on: the only signal is a GC-time RuntimeWarning (see The idea).
  • ❌ "await means run this in parallel"
    ✅ It means run this now and suspend me until it's done.
    ↳ So: concurrency comes from several tasks awaited together (tasks).
  • 🔀 Not the same as a Task
    ↳ Difference: a coroutine is a paused computation; a Task is the loop's driver that runs it concurrently.
  • ⚠️ Don't make a function async def if it never awaits.
    ↳ Why: callers must await it for nothing, and sync code can't call it at all.
  • ⚠️ Don't use asyncio.run() as a sync wrapper inside a library.
    ↳ Why: it raises cannot be called from a running event loop in notebooks and async frameworks.
    ↳ Instead: separate sync and async clients over a shared core.
  • 🔖 Version: async/await 3.5+ (PEP 492), async generators 3.6+ (PEP 525), @asyncio.coroutine removed in 3.11.
    ↳ Also: the "can't be awaited" error message changed in 3.14; checked on 3.12.13 and 3.14.6.

🕸️ Connections

Path: async execution model ─▶ async / await ─▶ tasks & cancellation ─▶ async primitives

  • Builds on generators and yield from: the suspended frame and the delegation await is made of.
  • Same mechanism as send / throw / close: coroutines inherit all three.
  • Used by tasks: a Task is the driver that calls send() for you.
  • Contrasts with threads: no function colouring, but a thread per wait.
  • Same idea elsewhere: JavaScript async functions return a Promise that runs eagerly; a Python coroutine doesn't start until awaited.

notes.title: Tasks, Gathering & Cancellation
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Creating tasks · 📘 Task groups · 📘 Task cancellation · 🔬 Notes on structured concurrency · 📖 Super Fast Python: asyncio guide

⚡ TL;DR

await runs one thing now; a task runs it alongside, independently of whoever started it. gather lets a failed fan-out leave its siblings running; TaskGroup cancels them and waits, so nothing outlives the block.

🧭 Flow: create_task schedules the coroutine at once ─▶ tasks overlap their waits ─▶ one fails ─▶ TaskGroup calls cancel() on the rest ─▶ each gets CancelledError at its current await ─▶ finally cleanup runs ─▶ the block raises an ExceptionGroup

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
await coro() vs create_task(coro())? Run it now and wait vs schedule it to run concurrently.
gather on the first failure? Raises it and does not cancel the others.
TaskGroup on the first failure? Cancels the rest, waits for them, raises an ExceptionGroup.
How is cancellation delivered? CancelledError thrown in at the task's current await; finally runs.
Why keep a reference to tasks? The loop holds only weak references; an unreferenced task can be collected mid-run.
✏️ Draw by hand: the cancellation path cancel() marks → CancelledError at the await → cleanup → cancelled; swallowed → finishes normally.

💡 The idea

Awaiting coroutines one after another runs them in sequence: five 100 ms calls take 0.50 s. Wrap each in a task and they overlap:

tasks = [asyncio.create_task(fetch(i)) for i in range(5)]   # all five start now
results = [await t for t in tasks]                          # → 0.10 s on CPython 3.12

The production question is what happens when one fails. Provider A raises at 50 ms and provider B takes 500 ms; run them with gather, then with a TaskGroup (traced on CPython 3.12):

Both surfaced the error at 50 ms. gather left B running for another 450 ms, holding its connection; TaskGroup cancelled B, waited for its cleanup, then raised.

The trade: tasks buy overlap by letting work run independently of the code that started it, and structured concurrency (TaskGroup) takes back the guarantee that nothing outlives its parent.

⚙️ How it works

Cancellation is a request, delivered at an await; timeouts and TaskGroup both feed into it:

All four rules below verified on CPython 3.12:

Rule What actually happens
A task is a coroutine plus a driver create_task wraps it in a Task (a Future subclass) and schedules its first step; it runs even if nothing awaits it. The loop holds only weak references, so keep tasks in a TaskGroup or a set you own.
Cancellation is cooperative CancelledError is a BaseException, so except Exception doesn't catch it, but a bare except: does: a coroutine that swallows it returned normally with cancelled() False. Code with no await can't be cancelled until it awaits.
Timeouts are cancellation on a timer asyncio.timeout(0.1) (3.11+) cancels the inner work and raises TimeoutError at 0.10 s; since 3.11 asyncio.TimeoutError is TimeoutError.
The collection APIs differ on failure gather propagates the first error and cancels nothing (return_exceptions=True returns errors as values); TaskGroup cancels, waits, raises an [[09-idiomatic-structural/56-exception-groups|ExceptionGroup]]; wait(FIRST_COMPLETED) returns (done, pending) and cancels nothing; as_completed yields in finishing order.

💻 Code

The LLM-gateway race: ask several providers, take the first good answer within one deadline, and make sure the losers actually stop.

import asyncio

async def first_good(prompt: str, providers: dict, deadline_s: float = 8.0):
    tasks = {asyncio.create_task(call(prompt), name=n): n for n, call in providers.items()}
    try:
        async with asyncio.timeout(deadline_s):                  # one budget for the race
            pending = set(tasks)
            while pending:
                done, pending = await asyncio.wait(pending, return_when=asyncio.FIRST_COMPLETED)
                for t in done:
                    if not t.cancelled() and t.exception() is None and is_valid(t.result()):
                        return tasks[t], t.result()              # winner
        raise RuntimeError("no provider returned a valid answer")
    finally:
        for t in tasks: t.cancel()                               # request the losers stop
        await asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True)     # and wait until they have

cancel() only requests, so without the final gather the function returns while the losers still hold pooled connections. wait(FIRST_COMPLETED) lets a fast invalid answer lose to a slower valid one.

⚠️ Break it: the orphaned sibling, by itself.

import asyncio, time
log = []
async def a(): await asyncio.sleep(0.05); raise ValueError("A failed")
async def b():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.5); log.append("B finished after the request failed")
async def main():
    try: await asyncio.gather(a(), b())
    except ValueError: log.append("caller saw the error")
    await asyncio.sleep(0.6); print(log)
asyncio.run(main())
# look for: "B finished" appears AFTER the caller saw the error
# naive model predicts: B is cancelled because the operation failed

On CPython 3.12 it printed ['caller saw the error', 'B finished after the request failed']. Under load those orphans pile up until the connection pool runs dry.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: A task runs a coroutine concurrently, independently of the code that created it. For several concurrent calls I default to TaskGroup (3.11+): if one fails it cancels the rest, waits for them, and raises an ExceptionGroup. gather returns results in order but leaves the others running on failure. Cancellation is cooperative: CancelledError arrives at the task's next await, cleanup runs, and code can refuse it by swallowing it.

Q · Mechanism — Walk through task.cancel() to the task actually ending. cancel() records the request and cancels the future the task is waiting on, so it gets scheduled. On its next step asyncio throws CancelledError in at the suspended await; it unwinds like any exception, running finally and async with exits, and the task ends cancelled (the flowchart). A coroutine that never awaits can't be cancelled until it does, and one that swallows the error refuses it, which also breaks every timeout around it.

Q · Failure — A gateway fanned out to three providers with gather. One raised at once, yet connections to the slow provider piled up until the pool ran dry. Reconstruct it. gather propagated the first error and the handler returned, but the other calls kept running as orphans, each holding a pooled connection until its slow provider answered (the picture). Load made orphans accumulate faster than they finished. Fix: TaskGroup, or gather(return_exceptions=True) with a per-call timeout; plus per-provider connection limits and a metric of in-flight calls per provider.

Q · Design — Fan out to five LLM providers, stream the first good answer, degrade when providers hang. Losers must stop promptly or they eat the pools and rate limits the next request needs, so: race with wait(FIRST_COMPLETED) inside one asyncio.timeout, cancel and await every task in finally (the Code section). Bound each provider separately: its own connection limit and semaphore, a circuit breaker after repeated timeouts, and hedging instead of always calling all five. I'd watch in-flight calls per provider against request rate: rising in-flight at flat load means cancellation isn't reaching something.

⚖️ Compare

gather TaskGroup (3.11+) wait as_completed
Results list, input order each task's .result() (done, pending) finishing order
On first failure raises it; others keep running cancels others, waits, raises ExceptionGroup nothing: you inspect done raises when you reach it
Cancels siblings ❌ ✅ ❌ (you do it) ❌
Best for simple fan-out with return_exceptions=True the default first-wins, partial results results as they arrive

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "If one call in a gather fails, the others stop"
    ✅ gather raises the first error and leaves the rest running (see Break it).
    ↳ Fix: TaskGroup when a failure should stop the group.
  • 🪞 "task.cancel() stops the task immediately"
    ✅ It requests cancellation, delivered at the next await, and code can refuse it.
  • ⚠️ Don't catch CancelledError without re-raising.
    ↳ Why: a bare except: or except BaseException: makes the task uncancellable and breaks every timeout around it.
    ↳ Instead: clean up, then raise.
  • ⚠️ Don't create_task and drop the reference.
    ↳ Why: weak references only: it can be collected mid-run, and its errors are lost.
    ↳ Instead: a TaskGroup, or a set you hold.
  • ⚠️ Don't cancel() and return immediately.
    ↳ Why: the cancelled tasks are still unwinding, still holding connections.
    ↳ Instead: await asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True) after cancelling.
  • 🔀 Not the same as running concurrently: await
    ↳ Difference: await coro() runs one coroutine to completion; concurrency comes from tasks.
  • 🔖 Version: create_task 3.7+; TaskGroup, asyncio.timeout and except* 3.11+; eager task factories 3.12.
    ↳ Note: behaviour measured on CPython 3.12.13 and 3.14.6.

🕸️ Connections

Path: async / await ─▶ tasks & cancellation ─▶ async primitives ─▶ exception groups

  • Builds on the event loop: a task is a callback the loop steps whenever its future completes.
  • Same mechanism as context managers: a TaskGroup is a scope that owns what it starts, like with for resources.
  • Used by reliability mechanics: timeouts, hedging and circuit breakers are built on cancellation.
  • Breaks when combined with threads: a thread started by to_thread keeps running after its task is cancelled.
  • Same idea elsewhere: trio nurseries and Kotlin's structured coroutineScope, both of which cancel children when one fails.

notes.title: Bridging Sync ↔ Async
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Running in threads: to_thread · 📘 loop.run_in_executor · 📘 Scheduling from other threads · 📖 Developing with asyncio

⚡ TL;DR

Async → sync: await asyncio.to_thread(fn); a pool thread blocks instead of the loop, and cancelling stops the wait, not the thread. Sync → async: asyncio.run at the top, run_coroutine_threadsafe from other threads, never asyncio.run inside a running loop.

🧭 Flow: coroutine awaits to_thread(fn) ─▶ the loop submits fn to its default thread pool ─▶ the coroutine suspends, the loop keeps serving ─▶ fn blocks on a pool thread ─▶ done: call_soon_threadsafe sets the result ─▶ the coroutine resumes with it

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
Blocking call inside a coroutine: fix? await asyncio.to_thread(fn, …), or run_in_executor with your own pool.
Does cancelling a to_thread task stop the function? No: the task is cancelled, the thread runs fn to completion.
Calling async from a different thread? asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(coro, loop).result(); never asyncio.run in a running loop.

💡 The idea

Inside a coroutine, a sync call is just a call, and it runs on the loop's only thread:

def legacy_lookup(key):
    time.sleep(0.2); return key.upper()          # a 200 ms sync SDK call
async def handler(key):
    return legacy_lookup(key)                    # every other task waits 200 ms

That's the shared-fate blocking from the async execution model. Hand it to a pool thread instead:

async def handler(key):
    return await asyncio.to_thread(legacy_lookup, key)   # the loop stays free

Now the loop serves others during those 200 ms. But it's a thread pool: twenty concurrent calls took 0.41 s, two waves on the default 14 threads (min(32, cpu + 4) on a 10-core machine, CPython 3.12). And cancellation stops at the bridge: a to_thread task cancelled after 50 ms still finished its 300 ms of work. The other direction has its own wall: asyncio.run inside a running loop raises RuntimeError: asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop.

The trade: to_thread keeps the loop responsive by paying for a pool thread per blocking call, bounded by the pool size, still under the GIL, and impossible to cancel once it starts.

⚙️ How it works

One bridged call, end to end:

It's run_in_executor plus context. to_thread(fn, *args) is loop.run_in_executor(None, fn, *args) with the current contextvars copied in, so request-scoped trace IDs survive the hop. Pass your own executor instead of None for a bigger pool, or a ProcessPoolExecutor for CPU work, the only one that escapes the GIL.

Results come back through one thread-safe door. call_soon_threadsafe is the only safe way into a running loop from another thread, and it's also what run_coroutine_threadsafe uses to hand a coroutine to a loop and give the calling thread a [[06-concurrency-gil/36-concurrent-futures|concurrent.futures.Future]] to block on.

💻 Code

A service with a blocking SDK and a CPU-heavy function, without starving the loop or the pool:

import asyncio
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, ProcessPoolExecutor

BLOCKING_IO = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=64, thread_name_prefix="sdk")  # sized for waits
SDK_SLOTS = asyncio.Semaphore(64)                                          # queue in the loop
CPU = ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=4)                                   # off the GIL

async def lookup(key: str) -> str:
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    async with SDK_SLOTS:
        return await asyncio.wait_for(
            loop.run_in_executor(BLOCKING_IO, legacy_sdk.lookup, key),
            timeout=2.0)              # the caller stops waiting, but the thread runs on:
                                      # the SDK needs its OWN timeout too

async def score(doc: str) -> float:
    return await asyncio.get_running_loop().run_in_executor(CPU, heavy_score, doc)

A dedicated pool keeps a slow SDK from exhausting the default pool every to_thread in the process shares; the semaphore makes excess callers wait as cheap coroutines instead of pool work items.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: Async to sync: a blocking call in a coroutine freezes the loop, so await asyncio.to_thread(fn) runs it on a pool thread while the loop serves others; CPU work goes to a process pool via run_in_executor. Sync to async: asyncio.run at the top level, run_coroutine_threadsafe(coro, loop) from another thread. The limits: the pool is finite, the GIL still applies, and cancelling the task doesn't stop the thread.

Q · Mechanism — What are the bridge's limits? Cancellation stops at the thread: cancelling the awaiting task, by hand, by timeout or by client disconnect, stops the wait, but the function runs to completion, so every bridged call needs its own timeout. The GIL still applies: pure-Python CPU work on a pool thread competes with the loop thread. And the default pool is min(32, cpu + 4) threads shared by every to_thread in the process, so one slow dependency can occupy it all; give heavy dependencies their own executor and a semaphore.

⚖️ Compare

Direction Tool Runs where Cancellable? Use for
async → sync I/O asyncio.to_thread(fn, …) default thread pool the wait yes, the thread no occasional blocking I/O
async → sync I/O, heavy run_in_executor(my_pool, fn, …) your sized pool same a blocking SDK at volume
async → CPU run_in_executor(ProcessPoolExecutor, …) worker processes same, plus pickling CPU work off the GIL
sync → async, top level asyncio.run(coro) a new loop, this thread n/a scripts, CLIs, entry points
sync thread → running loop run_coroutine_threadsafe(coro, loop) that loop's thread future.cancel() callbacks from threads, GUIs

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "to_thread makes a blocking function async"
    ✅ It runs it on a pool thread: still blocking, still bounded by the pool, still under the GIL.
  • ❌ "wait_for(to_thread(fn), 2) stops fn after 2 seconds"
    ✅ It stops waiting after 2 seconds; fn keeps running.
    ↳ Fix: give fn its own timeout.
  • 🔀 Not the same as non-blocking
    ↳ Difference: an async client yields while it waits; to_thread makes a different thread block instead.
    ↳ So: only the async client scales to thousands of concurrent calls.
  • ⚠️ Don't use to_thread for pure-Python CPU work.
    ↳ Why: it still contends for the GIL with the loop thread.
    ↳ Instead: a process pool.
  • ⚠️ Don't share the default executor with a slow dependency.
    ↳ Why: it can occupy every pool thread and stall unrelated to_thread calls.
    ↳ Instead: a dedicated executor plus a semaphore.
  • ⚠️ Don't call asyncio.run from async code or a library.
    ↳ Instead: await the coroutine, or run_coroutine_threadsafe from another thread.
  • 🔖 Version: to_thread 3.9+; asyncio.Runner 3.11+; default pool size uses os.process_cpu_count() from 3.13.
    ↳ Note: timings measured on CPython 3.12.13 and 3.14.6, 10-core machine.

🕸️ Connections

Path: async execution model ─▶ bridging sync and async ─▶ async primitives

  • Builds on concurrent.futures: the executors and futures the bridge is made of.
  • Breaks when combined with cancellation: it reaches the coroutine but never the thread.
  • Contrasts with the GIL: threads help waiting, not computing; CPU work needs processes.
  • Used by async primitives: a semaphore in front of every bridged dependency.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Node's libuv thread pool runs blocking file and DNS work off the event loop the same way.

notes.title: Async Primitives & Patterns
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 asyncio synchronization primitives · 📘 asyncio queues · 📜 PEP 525: async generators · 📖 Super Fast Python: asyncio guide

⚡ TL;DR

In async code, races live across await points: an asyncio.Lock covers the gap. A Semaphore caps what runs; a bounded Queue caps what waits, and that wait is backpressure.

🧭 Flow: a check-then-act with an await in between ─▶ other tasks run in the gap ─▶ several pass the check before any acts ─▶ async with lock covers the whole sequence ─▶ a Semaphore caps calls in flight ─▶ a bounded Queue makes producers wait for consumers

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
Why does single-threaded async need a Lock? Any await inside a check-then-act lets other tasks run in the gap.
Semaphore vs bounded Queue? Caps concurrent operations vs caps buffered items, making producers wait.
Are asyncio primitives thread-safe? No: bound to one loop; use call_soon_threadsafe or queue.Queue across threads.

💡 The idea

Between two awaits nothing can interleave, so a check-then-act with no await is safe. Real code awaits in the middle, a database read or an audit write:

balance = {"v": 100}
async def withdraw(name, n):
    if balance["v"] >= n:                # check
        await record_audit(n)            # ← suspension point
        balance["v"] -= n                # act

Three concurrent withdraw(100) calls, traced on CPython 3.12:

Step Task Does balance
1 A check passes, then awaits the audit 100
2 B (A suspended) check passes, awaits 100
3 C check passes, awaits 100
4–6 A, B, C each debits after its await 0 → −100 → −200

An asyncio.Lock held across the whole sequence (async with lock: around check, await and debit) left it at 0: B and C saw 0 and did nothing. The other two primitives control how much runs: a Semaphore(3) capped twelve 50 ms calls at three in flight (0.20 s, four waves), and a Queue(maxsize=2) made a fast producer wait for a 50 ms consumer, its put waits measuring [0, 0, 0, 51, 51, 51] ms. That wait is backpressure.

The trade: the async primitives make an invariant hold across await points and put limits on concurrency, at the cost of explicit scoping, which is exactly what makes them easy to forget.

⚙️ How it works

A bounded pipeline stage, where both limits meet:

Built on futures, not OS locks. Waiting on a Lock, Semaphore, Event, Condition or full Queue suspends the coroutine on a future and frees the loop; a release wakes the next waiter in FIFO order. They belong to one loop and are not thread-safe.

async with and async for make them ergonomic. __aenter__/__aexit__ and __aiter__/__anext__ may await; an async generator abandoned mid-iteration needs aclose() (or contextlib.aclosing) for its finally to run.

💻 Code

A bounded stage: backpressure from the queue, a cap on the downstream, structured shutdown.

import asyncio

async def pipeline(source, handle, workers: int = 8, max_in_flight: int = 16):
    queue: asyncio.Queue = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=workers * 2)   # bounded: producer slows down
    downstream = asyncio.Semaphore(max_in_flight)              # cap on calls to the dependency

    async def produce():
        async for item in source:
            await queue.put(item)                              # suspends while full
        for _ in range(workers):
            await queue.put(None)                              # one sentinel per worker

    async def work():
        while (item := await queue.get()) is not None:
            try:
                async with downstream:
                    await handle(item)
            finally:
                queue.task_done()

    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:                      # any failure cancels the stage
        tg.create_task(produce())
        for _ in range(workers):
            tg.create_task(work())

maxsize bounds memory however big the source is; the semaphore separates "how many workers" from "how many calls the downstream sees". On 3.13+, queue.shutdown() replaces the sentinels.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: Async code runs on one thread, but a task can suspend at any await, and others run in the gap. So a check-then-act with an await inside races: three concurrent withdrawals left a balance at −200. An asyncio.Lock across the whole sequence fixes it. A Semaphore caps concurrent operations against a downstream, and a bounded Queue makes producers wait for consumers, which is backpressure.

Q · Mechanism — Design a producer/consumer stage with backpressure. What breaks with an unbounded queue? A producer feeds an asyncio.Queue(maxsize=N), fixed workers consume it, and a semaphore wraps the downstream call (the flowchart). When workers fall behind, the queue fills and put suspends, so the slow part sets the pace and memory is bounded. With an unbounded queue nothing pushes back: a burst or a slow dependency grows the queue until the process is OOMKilled, and every item's latency grows with queue depth. Bounded queues turn overload into visible upstream slowdowns.

⚖️ Compare

Primitive Protects or limits Typical use
asyncio.Lock one task inside a check-await-update section balances, lazy init, cache fills
asyncio.Semaphore(N) at most N concurrent holders calls to a downstream or provider
asyncio.Queue(maxsize=N) at most N buffered items; producers wait pipelines, worker pools
asyncio.Event a one-shot signal many tasks wait on "ready", "shutting down"
asyncio.Condition / Barrier (3.11+) a predicate on shared state / N tasks meet coordination, phased work

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "asyncio is single-threaded, so there are no races"
    ✅ Races happen across await points (see the trace table).
  • ❌ "asyncio.Lock and threading.Lock are interchangeable"
    ✅ asyncio.Lock suspends one coroutine; threading.Lock blocks the thread.
    ↳ So: a threading.Lock in a coroutine blocks the whole event loop.
  • 🔀 Not the same: Semaphore and bounded Queue
    ↳ Difference: a semaphore limits what is running; a bounded queue limits what is waiting.
    ↳ So: pipelines usually need both.
  • ⚠️ Don't use unbounded queues between stages.
    ↳ Why: a slow consumer turns into unbounded memory growth.
    ↳ Instead: set maxsize and export queue depth.
  • ⚠️ Don't hold an asyncio.Lock across slow external calls unless the invariant needs it.
    ↳ Why: every task waiting on it stalls for the whole call.
    ↳ Instead: narrow the critical section.
  • ⚠️ Don't abandon an async generator mid-iteration.
    ↳ Why: its finally waits for garbage collection.
    ↳ Instead: aclose() or contextlib.aclosing.
  • 🔖 Version: the loop= argument was removed in 3.10; Barrier 3.11+; Queue.shutdown() 3.13+.
    ↳ Note: behaviour measured on CPython 3.12.13 and 3.14.6.

🕸️ Connections

Path: tasks & cancellation ─▶ async primitives ─▶ rate limiting / background workers

  • Same mechanism as synchronization hazards: the same races and lock rules, with await points where threads have switch points.
  • Builds on the event loop: every wait here is a future the loop resumes.
  • Used by rate limiting and streaming transport: semaphores and bounded buffers in production.
  • Contrasts with threading primitives: those block threads; these suspend coroutines.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Go's buffered channels give the same backpressure: a send blocks when the buffer is full.

notes.title: Async Ecosystem & Comparatives
notes.html:
📚 References

🔧 uvloop · 🔧 anyio documentation

⚡ TL;DR

uvloop swaps the loop (faster I/O), anyio swaps the API (asyncio or trio), trio swaps the whole model (structured first). Async wins at many I/O waits; for CPU work none of them help: use processes.

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
What does uvloop speed up? Loop and socket overhead (libuv), about 2× on echo round-trips; not your Python code.
asyncio vs trio vs anyio? Stdlib loop / a structured-concurrency library / one API over both.
Selecting uvloop on 3.12+? asyncio.run(main(), loop_factory=uvloop.new_event_loop); loop policies are deprecated in 3.14.

💡 The idea

asyncio.run(main()) runs on the stdlib loop, mostly Python over selectors, and both the loop and the API are replaceable. uvloop is a drop-in loop on libuv (Node's library): 20,000 socket echo round-trips took 0.50 s vs 1.10 s on the default loop (uvloop 0.22.1, CPython 3.12), but 200,000 no-op coroutines ran about the same, so it helps I/O-heavy loops only. trio is built around structured concurrency (nurseries, cancel scopes), the idea asyncio's [[07-async-io/42-tasks-gather-cancellation|TaskGroup]] borrowed in 3.11. anyio is one API over either, so a library runs on both. Async beats threads for many concurrent waits and loses to processes for CPU work (concurrency vs parallelism).

💻 Code

import asyncio, uvloop, anyio
async def main():
    async with anyio.create_task_group() as tg:      # anyio API: asyncio or trio underneath
        tg.start_soon(anyio.sleep, 0.1)
    return type(asyncio.get_running_loop()).__name__
print(asyncio.run(main(), loop_factory=uvloop.new_event_loop))   # → Loop (uvloop's)
